method: Each claim checked against the retrieved text of the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard page (2019 Standard; page last updated 30 April 2026), including the six quality statements, the full indicator list and the cultural safety and equity section. The Standard names no drug or dose; aspirin, DAPT, lipid-lowering therapy, beta blockers and ACE inhibitors appear only as indicator categories and nothing is asserted about agent or dose. The Commission's own statement that the Standard has not been updated against the 2025 NHFA/CSANZ guidelines is recorded verbatim and flagged time_sensitive. RE-VERIFIED 2026-09-22: the page recorded in retrieved_from was fetched again and every claim attributed to this source was re-checked against it with scripts/verify.py. Quotes stored from the earlier scrape carried that scrape's markdown artifacts (** emphasis, bullet joins glued on as 'n- ', table pipes) and, in some words containing a doubled n, a lost letter ('planned' stored as 'pla ed'). Those fragments were not verbatim with respect to the source document. Each was replaced with the text the page actually carries, located by alignment against the retrieved copy (scripts/repair_quotes.py), not reconstructed from memory.

claims.claim: The Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard was first published in 2014 and last reviewed against the guidelines in 2019, and includes six quality statements describing safe and appropriate care and a set of indicators to support monitoring and quality improvement
claims.source_text: The Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard was first published in 2014 and last reviewed against the guidelines in 2019. The Standard includes: - six quality statements describing safe and appropriate care - a set of indicators to support monitoring and quality improvement

claims.claim: Key evidence sources underpinning the Standard are the Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand Australian Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes 2016, those guidelines were updated in 2025, and the Standard has not been updated against the 2025 guidelines
claims.source_text: Key evidence sources that underpin the Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard are clinical guidelines from the Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Australian Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes 2016. Note that these clinical guidelines were updated in 2025. The Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard has not been updated against the 2025 guidelines.

claims.claim: The Commission has commenced a review of the 2019 Standard to ensure it aligns with the latest evidence-based guidance and clinical practice, and it is anticipated that the updated Standard will be finalised in late 2027
claims.source_text: The Commission has commenced a review of the Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard (2019) to ensure that the Standard aligns with the latest evidence-based guidance and clinical practice. ... It is anticipated that the updated Standard will be finalised in late 2027.

claims.claim: Coronary heart disease, the main cause of acute coronary syndromes, kills more people in Australia than any other disease
claims.source_text: Coronary heart disease (the main cause of acute coronary syndromes) kills more people in Australia than any other disease.

claims.claim: While there are well-developed guidelines for managing acute coronary syndromes, not all people receive appropriate treatment and there is variation in the type of care received across Australia
claims.source_text: While there are well-developed guidelines for managing acute coronary syndromes, not all people receive appropriate treatment and there is variation in the type of care received across Australia.

claims.claim: Acute coronary syndromes include ST elevation myocardial infarction, non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, and unstable angina, which is chest pain usually due to restricted blood flow to the heart muscle and can lead to a heart attack
claims.source_text: Acute coronary syndromes include ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and unstable angina (chest pain usually due to restricted blood flow to the heart muscle), which can lead to a heart attack.

claims.claim: An acute coronary syndrome results from a sudden blockage of a blood vessel in the heart typically by a thrombosis that reduces blood supply to a portion of heart muscle, and if the blockage is severe enough to lead to injury or death of the heart muscle the event is called an acute myocardial infarction
claims.source_text: An acute coronary syndrome (ACS) results from a sudden blockage of a blood vessel in the heart, typically by a blood clot (thrombosis) that reduces blood supply to a portion of heart muscle. If the blockage is severe enough to lead to injury or death of the heart muscle, the event is called an acute myocardial infarction (or heart attack).

claims.claim: The most common cause of an acute coronary syndrome is atherosclerosis, in which an artery wall thickens as a result of a build-up of fatty materials such as cholesterol
claims.source_text: The most common cause of an ACS is atherosclerosis (or coronary heart disease), in which an artery wall thickens as a result of a build-up of fatty materials such as cholesterol.

claims.claim: Quality statement 1 states that a patient presenting with acute chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome receives care guided by a documented chest pain assessment pathway
claims.source_text: A patient presenting with acute chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome receives care guided by a documented chest pain assessment pathway.

claims.claim: Clinicians should use a documented chest pain assessment pathway to provide care to all patients who present with symptoms of an ACS and ensure that patients understand what is happening and why
claims.source_text: Use a documented chest pain assessment pathway to provide care to all patients who present with symptoms of an ACS. Ensure that your patients understand what is happening and why.

claims.claim: A chest pain assessment pathway taken from the national guideline is available from the Heart Foundation
claims.source_text: A chest pain assessment pathway taken from the national guideline is available from the Heart Foundation

claims.claim: Quality statement 2 states that a patient with acute chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome receives a 12-lead electrocardiogram and the results are analysed by a clinician experienced in interpreting an ECG within 10 minutes of the first emergency clinical contact
claims.source_text: A patient with acute chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome receives a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), and the results are analysed by a clinician experienced in interpreting an ECG within 10 minutes of the first emergency clinical contact.

claims.claim: Assessing all patients with a suspected ACS with a 12-lead ECG and interpreting the results within 10 minutes of the first emergency clinical contact may involve facilitating referral to a clinician experienced in performing or interpreting an ECG
claims.source_text: Assess all patients with a suspected ACS with a 12-lead ECG, and interpret the results within 10 minutes of the first emergency clinical contact. This may involve facilitating referral to a clinician experienced in performing or interpreting an ECG.

claims.claim: Quality statement 3 states that a patient with an acute ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction for whom emergency reperfusion is clinically appropriate is offered timely percutaneous coronary intervention or fibrinolysis in accordance with the timeframes recommended in the current National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand guidelines
claims.source_text: A patient with an acute ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), for whom emergency reperfusion is clinically appropriate, is offered timely percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or fibrinolysis in accordance with the time frames recommended in the current National Heart Foundation of Australia/Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes.

claims.claim: In general primary PCI is recommended if the time from first medical contact to balloon inflation is anticipated to be less than 90 minutes, otherwise the patient is offered fibrinolysis
claims.source_text: In general, primary PCI is recommended if the time from first medical contact to balloon inflation is anticipated to be less than 90 minutes; otherwise, the patient is offered fibrinolysis.

claims.claim: Clinicians should offer primary PCI or fibrinolysis to all eligible patients diagnosed with an acute STEMI within the recommended timeframes and ensure the patient understands the risks and benefits of their proposed treatment and provides their consent
claims.source_text: Offer primary PCI or fibrinolysis to all eligible patients diagnosed with an acute STEMI, within the time frames recommended in the current Heart Foundation of Australia/Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes. Ensure that the patient understands the risks and benefits of their proposed treatment, and provides their consent.

claims.claim: Quality statement 4 states that a patient with a non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndrome is managed based on a documented evidence-based assessment of their risk of an adverse event
claims.source_text: A patient with a non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEACS) is managed based on a documented, evidence-based assessment of their risk of an adverse event.

claims.claim: Clinicians should use an evidence-based risk assessment tool to stratify the patient's risk of future cardiac events, discuss the identified level of risk with the patient, and use a shared decision making process to plan treatment based on their risk of an adverse event and their treatment preferences
claims.source_text: Use an evidence-based risk assessment tool to stratify the patient's risk of future cardiac events. Discuss the identified level of risk with the patient, and use a shared decision making process to plan their treatment based on their risk of an adverse event and their treatment preferences.

claims.claim: Risk assessment tools named include the GRACE ACS Risk Calculator, the TIMI Risk Score for UA/NSTEMI, and Decision making and timing considerations in reperfusion for STEMI
claims.source_text: Risk assessment tools include: - GRACE ACS Risk Calculator 2 - TIMI Risk Score for UA/NSTEMI 3 - Decision making and timing considerations in reperfusion for STEMI

claims.claim: Quality statement 5 states that the role of coronary angiography, with a view to timely and appropriate coronary revascularisation, is discussed with a patient with a non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndrome who is assessed to be at intermediate or high risk of an adverse cardiac event
claims.source_text: The role of coronary angiography, with a view to timely and appropriate coronary revascularisation, is discussed with a patient with a non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEACS) who is assessed to be at intermediate or high risk of an adverse cardiac event.

claims.claim: If patients are identified to be at intermediate or high risk of an adverse cardiac event clinicians should discuss with them the risks and benefits of coronary angiography and appropriate revascularisation
claims.source_text: If patients are identified to be at intermediate or high risk of an adverse cardiac event, discuss with them the risks and benefits of coronary angiography and appropriate revascularisation.

claims.claim: Quality statement 6 states that before a patient with an acute coronary syndrome leaves hospital they are involved in the development of an individualised care plan identifying the lifestyle modifications and medicines needed to manage their risk factors, addressing their psychosocial needs and including a referral to an appropriate cardiac rehabilitation or another secondary prevention program, and that this plan is provided to the patient and their general practitioner or ongoing clinical provider within 48 hours of discharge
claims.source_text: Before a patient with an acute coronary syndrome leaves the hospital, they are involved in the development of an individualised care plan. This plan identifies the lifestyle modifications and medicines needed to manage their risk factors, addresses their psychosocial needs and includes a referral to an appropriate cardiac rehabilitation or another secondary prevention program. This plan is provided to the patient and their general practitioner or ongoing clinical provider within 48 hours of discharge.

claims.claim: Indicator 1a is the proportion of patients presenting with symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome whose care is guided by a documented chest pain assessment pathway
claims.source_text: Indicator 1a Proportion of patients presenting with symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) whose care is guided by a documented chest pain assessment pathway

claims.claim: Indicator 2a is the proportion of patients with symptoms suggestive of acute coronary syndrome with an electrocardiogram performed and interpreted within 10 minutes of first clinical contact
claims.source_text: Indicator 2a Proportion of patients with symptoms suggestive of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) with an electrocardiogram (ECG) performed and interpreted within 10 minutes of first clinical contact

claims.claim: Indicator 3b is the proportion of patients with STEMI receiving fibrinolysis before or within 30 minutes of hospital presentation, and indicator 3c is the proportion treated with percutaneous coronary intervention within 90 minutes of first clinical contact
claims.source_text: Indicator 3b Proportion of patients with ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) receiving fibrinolysis before or within 30 minutes of hospital presentation Indicator 3c Proportion of patients with ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 90 minutes of first clinical contact

claims.claim: Indicator 4a is the proportion of patients with NSTEACS who have a documented assessment and risk stratification using a guideline-recommended tool, and indicator 4b is the proportion of NSTEACS patients transferred to a hospital with angiography facilities
claims.source_text: Indicator 4a Proportion of patients with non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEACS) who have a documented assessment and risk stratification using a guideline-recommended tool Indicator 4b Proportion of patients with non-ST-segment-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEACS) transferred to a hospital with angiography facilities

claims.claim: Indicator 6b is the proportion of patients with acute coronary syndrome on aspirin or dual antiplatelet therapy on separation from hospital, and indicator 6c is the proportion prescribed lipid-lowering therapy on separation
claims.source_text: Indicator 6b Proportion of patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) on aspirin or dual antiplatelet therapy on separation from hospital Indicator 6c Proportion of patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) prescribed lipid-lowering therapy on separation from hospital

claims.claim: Indicator 6d is the proportion of patients with myocardial infarction who had their left ventricular ejection fraction measured prior to separation from hospital, and indicator 6e is the proportion of patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction prescribed a beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor on separation
claims.source_text: Indicator 6d Proportion of patients with myocardial infarction who had their left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) measured prior to separation from hospital Indicator 6e Proportion of patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) prescribed a beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor on separation from hospital

claims.claim: Indicator 6f is the proportion of patients with acute coronary syndrome referred to cardiac rehabilitation or other secondary prevention program, and indicator 6g is the proportion whose discharge summary was provided to their general practitioner or ongoing clinical provider within 48 hours of separation
claims.source_text: Indicator 6f Proportion of patients with acute coronary syndrome referred to cardiac rehabilitation or other secondary prevention program Indicator 6g Proportion of patients with acute coronary syndrome whose discharge summary was provided to their general practitioner or ongoing clinical provider within 48 hours of separation from hospital

claims.claim: No benchmarks are set for these indicators by the Commission and definitions required to collect and calculate indicator data are specified online at METEOR
claims.source_text: No benchmarks are set for these indicators by the Commission. When using the indicators, please refer to the definitions required to collect and calculate indicator data which are specified online at METEOR.

claims.claim: The Standard relates to the care that patients with a suspected ACS receive from the onset of symptoms to the completion of their treatment in hospital and includes patients who develop a suspected ACS while in hospital for another condition
claims.source_text: This Standard relates to the care that patients with a suspected ACS receive from the onset of symptoms to the completion of their treatment in hospital. It includes patients who develop a suspected ACS while in hospital for another condition.

claims.claim: In rural and remote settings different strategies may be needed to implement the standard, for example hub-and-spoke models integrating larger and smaller health services and ACCHOs, telehealth consultations, and multidisciplinary teams including allied health involvement where clinically appropriate
claims.source_text: In rural and remote settings, different strategies may be needed to implement the standard. For example, the use of: - hub‑and‑spoke models integrating larger and smaller health services and ACCHOs - telehealth consultations - multidisciplinary teams including allied health involvement where clinically appropriate

claims.claim: The Standard has been endorsed by the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine, the Australian College of Rural and Remote Medicine, CRANA plus, Heart Foundation Australia and the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons
claims.source_text: The Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard has been endorsed by five key health organisations. - Australasian College for Emergency Medicine - Australian College of Rural and Remote Medicine - CRANA plus - Heart Foundation Australia - Royal Australasian College of Surgeons

claims.claim: Health outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples can be improved by addressing systemic racism and other root causes that reduce access to care, with historical and current contributing factors including a lack of culturally safe care, culturally appropriate health education and sociocultural determinants such as differences in employment opportunities
claims.source_text: Health outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples can be improved by addressing systemic racism and other root causes that reduce access to care. Historical and current contributing factors include a lack of culturally safe care, culturally appropriate health education and sociocultural determinants such as differences in employment opportunities.

claims.claim: Cultural safety and equity recommendations were developed in consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander individuals, clinicians and representative health service organisations, however it is recognised that cultural safety is determined by the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander individuals, families and communities experiencing the care
claims.source_text: Cultural safety and equity recommendations in this document have been developed in consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander individuals, clinicians and representative health service organisations. However, it is recognised that cultural safety is determined by the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander individuals, families and communities experiencing the care.

claims.claim: Building culturally safe systems includes ensuring systems and processes support people to self-report their Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status and to record self-identification, ensuring all staff engage regularly in cultural safety training, disaggregating data by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status when using the indicators to support identification of access and outcome issues, and implementing the six actions for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health from the NSQHS Standards
claims.source_text: Ensure systems and processes support people to self-report their Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status and to record self-identification. - Ensure all staff engage regularly in cultural safety training. - Disaggregate data by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status when using the indicators included in this Standard. This will support identification of access and outcome issues so that improvements can be made. - Implement the six actions for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health from the NSQHS Standards

claims.claim: Flexible and connected service delivery includes providing flexible service delivery to optimise attendance and help develop trust, establishing robust communication channels and referral pathways with primary healthcare providers including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled Health Organisations, and where possible providing outreach services close to home, on Country or in collaboration with ACCHOs or other community healthcare providers
claims.source_text: Provide flexible service delivery to optimise attendance and help develop trust with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander individuals and communities. - Establish robust communication channels and referral pathways with primary healthcare providers, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled Health Organisations (ACCHOs). - Where possible, provide outreach services close to home, on Country or in collaboration with ACCHOs or other community healthcare providers

claims.claim: Communication and person-centred care includes taking a collaborative approach to tailor interventions to the individual's needs and preferences, encouraging the inclusion of support people, family and kin and the person's trusted healthcare provider such as their ACCHO in all aspects of care including decision making, engaging culturally appropriate interpreter services and cultural translators, involving Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Workers or Health Practitioners in the multidisciplinary team and Liaison Officers in hospital settings, and using culturally and linguistically appropriate materials accounting for varying levels of health literacy
claims.source_text: Take a collaborative approach to ensure that interventions are suitably tailored to the individual's personal needs and preferences for care. - Encourage the inclusion of support people, family and kin, and the person's trusted healthcare provider (such as their ACCHO) in all aspects of care, including decision making and plans for treatment and management. - Engage culturally appropriate interpreter services and cultural translators when this will assist the patient. - Involve Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Workers or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioners as part of a patient's multidisciplinary team and involve Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Liaison Officers in hospital settings. - Use culturally and linguistically appropriate materials to aid in communication and discussion, accounting for varying levels of health literacy

claims.claim: The Better Cardiac Care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People project has also informed the development of the Standard and provides national recommendations for better cardiac care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
claims.source_text: The Better Cardiac Care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People project has also informed the development of the Standard. The Better Cardiac Care project provides national recommendations for better cardiac care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

claims.claim: The Standard applies to care provided in acute hospital settings including public and private hospitals, and not all quality statements will be applicable to every healthcare service or clinical unit
claims.source_text: This Standard applies to care provided in acute hospital settings, including public and private hospitals. Not all quality statements in this Standard will be applicable to every healthcare service or clinical unit.
